doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Label, collaborations and the working artist
title: Surviving financially and arts advocacy
summary: Declining composer incomes, the Robeson tribute as curriculum, the incubator model, and making the case for the arts.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: As a parent, you are a parent and have a family, you have realistic living expenses and so forth, which part of your role as an artist helps you survive the most?

Well it’s different every year. In May, I think it was a May issue of Time magazine there was a list of occupations that had wage slashes and the top one was I think auctioneers. I think it was something like over 90 thousand to 45 thousand. And composers were the second, somewhere around 90 thousand to 45 thousand. So I mean yeah, this year it’s really slow. But you know in some ways artists, we’re able to deal with the fluidity of the economy. Especially people like me who improvise. I mean you improvise in the music but you have to improvise and sort of have a creative, well be creative and sophisticated to be able to support your work and your family. So some of it is looking, see I spoke about the non-profit arts world. But some of it is looking at market hybridity and trying to, you know like for example the work “A Musical Tribute to Paul Robeson: When Sorrow Turns to Joy” that James Newton and I composed, the story of Paul Robeson and his contributions that we discovered could be made into curriculum materials for the high schools, for colleges. So ideas like that. And I think that for us, our strength, artists as catalysts, is that we can incubate like new work and ideas. And that’s not only, well that’s a powerful tool in these artists-in-residency. But that’s something that’s translatable in the business world when they incubate ideas and so forth. A model of that which I think I read it was incorporated, they had an interview with Robert Redford and it was a great interview where he described the incubator process and how that, you know what we’re faced in this country is an idea drought and how Sundance played an important role in creating this process, this laboratory, into developing these independent films which also created, I mean aside from it being important values to our country, and I guess that’s the other part that Robert Redford said about economic development. He’s not only concerned about revenue, which they were successful at, but the quality of revenue. So I think that’s what we bring to this table is that when we invest in something like the music that we’re creating and there should be an awareness of the quality of the revenue. I mean in other words this non-profit arts organization that I co-founded, we share a building with an organization called Justice Matters, which is not an arts organization. But they support us, providing us technical assistance, web support and space, because their clients see that they’re not about making money. That they are part of something with people that are compassionate and it’s not all about money but about art and creating a societal change. And so that’s what, that’s why we have to be proactive. Because a lot of times © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

what’s a weakness in arts advocacy — because in some ways it’s been set up to be an entitlement program. And we’re just learning I think artists, arts makers, arts administrators, foundations and funders are just beginning to learn how do we articulate ourselves to be able to win people over, the public opinion. So and one way is how arts does, for every dollar that’s put in the arts, eight dollars is developed out of that. And arts helps build tourism, it creates other jobs with restaurants, hotels, taxicab drivers and so forth. So that’s why I think the other part of Jon Jang is that we have to look at our art in relationship to our life and our public and our communities. And the other part of it is that I’m part of some important physical and historical communities in San Francisco Chinatown, in Japantown, and Oakland Chinatown. And those are very important experiences because we bring young people to these places so that they’re not like isolated in say white suburbs and you know all the whole world is that block. And it’s not just I think Chinese-Americans, but also other people. Because that’s part of I mean Chinese-American and Japanese-American history is part of American history. So then for people who are not of those nationalities I think that’s important for them to know, for them to understand their experiences as Americans.
